540.title: Service of the heart (Taanit 2a)
540.hook: the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart
540.howItsDone: Jewish law asks for kavanah, focused intention, especially in the first line of the Shema and the first blessing of the Amidah, which is said quietly, lips moving, in the manner learned from Hannah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three times a day: morning, afternoon and evening, the hinges of the day. Did you find your three pauses? Today, what prayer is, in two Hebrew words. Day five hundred forty.

The Shema, said twice a day, includes a paragraph from Deuteronomy that asks people to serve God with all their heart. Serve how, exactly? You can serve with your hands. You can build, carry, cook, bring an offering to an altar. That's what service meant in the Temple: real, physical work. But serve with your heart? You can't hand someone your heart on a plate. The Talmud stops at that phrase and asks exactly that question.
screen: `SERVE WITH YOUR HANDS.` → `BUILD, CARRY, COOK, OFFER.` → `BUT WITH YOUR HEART?`

segments.voice: The verse is Deuteronomy eleven: "to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." At the opening of tractate Taanit, the Talmud asks: what is service that is in the heart? And it answers: this is prayer. Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. Avodah is the same word used for the priests' work in the Temple: the offerings, the incense, the daily routine. So the phrase makes a bold claim. Prayer is real service, standing alongside the Temple's. After the Temple was destroyed, that idea carried enormous weight. The prophet Hosea had already put it in a single line: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words in place of offerings. Where does the heart come in? The rabbis learned much about how to pray from Hannah, at the start of the book of Samuel, praying for a child. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The Talmud learns from her that prayer needs the heart directed, the lips moving, and the voice kept low. Jewish tradition has a word for that directing of the heart: kavanah, intention. The siddur supplies the words. The heart has to do the work of meaning them. That's why it's called service. It isn't only a feeling. It's effort, like any other work.
screen: `SERVE WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `AVODAH: THE TEMPLE'S WORK.` · `THE OFFERING OF OUR LIPS.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, VOICE UNHEARD.` · then, large: `PRAYER IS THE HEART'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one heartfelt sentence. Settle, and breathe. Let one sentence rise from somewhere honest in you. It could be thanks, a worry, a hope, a name. If you pray, it can be to God, in your own words. If you don't, it can be said to no one, or to the quiet. Say it the way Hannah did: lips moving, voice barely there. Then say it once more, slower, and mean every word. The bell holds the time.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. The Talmud's name for prayer.
Your line: prayer is the heart's work. Today, out of the words you say on autopilot, mean one sentence completely. Day five hundred forty.

541.title: Entering the room
541.hook: Balaam's words "how goodly are thy tents" are said on entering a synagogue
541.howItsDone: Many Jews say mah tovu (Numbers 24:5) on entering a synagogue in the morning, followed by verses from the Psalms; in many siddurim it is the first passage of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev, the service of the heart. Your line was prayer is the heart's work. Which sentence did you mean completely? Today, the siddur's first words for many people, said at the door. Day five hundred forty-one.

Doorways change people. You lower your voice walking into a library. You straighten your back at the door of a job interview. At some homes you take your shoes off before you're even asked. Something in us knows a threshold is a small border. In many synagogues, the first words people say on entering come from a surprising source. They were first spoken by a foreign prophet who had been hired to curse.
screen: `QUIET IN THE LIBRARY.` → `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `WORDS FROM A HIRED PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Back in Numbers, King Balak of Moab hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam climbs a height, looks down at the camp spread across the valley, tribe by tribe, and blessing comes out of his mouth instead: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, mah tovu: how good. What did he see down there? The Talmud, in Bava Batra, and Rashi after it, point to a detail. The tents were set up so that no doorway faced another doorway. Each family had its privacy. A huge camp, and no one peering into anyone else's home. The respect was visible from the hilltop. Tradition read tents and dwellings as more than tents. The rabbis took them as houses of prayer and houses of study. So the verse became words for entering a synagogue. In many siddurim, mah tovu stands at the very beginning of the morning prayers, followed by a psalm verse about coming into God's house through God's great kindness. There's a twist worth noticing. These are the words of an outsider, someone sent to do harm, who looked closely and saw goodness. A few later teachers were uneasy about opening prayer with Balaam's words. The custom stayed. Many find it moving that the prayer book begins with what a stranger saw: a community that respects one another's doors.
screen: `BALAAM, HIRED TO CURSE.` · `MAH TOVU: HOW GOOD.` · `NO DOOR FACING ANOTHER.` · `AN OUTSIDER'S WORDS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `HOW GOOD THESE TENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause at one doorway. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next doorway you'll walk through: a home, a classroom, an office, a place of worship. See yourself stopping just before it, for a single breath. If you pray, mah tovu is there: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob. If not, simply notice what's good about the place you're about to enter, and about the people inside it. Then picture stepping through. The bell holds the time.
Entering the room. Mah tovu, how good: Balaam's blessing, said at the synagogue door.
Your line: how good these tents. Today, before you walk into one room, pause and find one good thing about it, or its people. Day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: The morning blessings
542.hook: a chain of thanks for waking: sight, clothing, standing upright
542.howItsDone: Many Jews say the morning blessings at the start of the weekday and Shabbat morning service, often led aloud by the prayer leader with the congregation answering amen, and some say them at home on waking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the doorway, and Balaam's words said on entering a synagogue. Your line was how good these tents. Which doorway did you pause at? Today, the very first prayers of the morning. Day five hundred forty-two.

Before coffee, before the phone, before anyone has said a word to you, a lot has already gone right. Your eyes opened. You could tell it was morning. You sat up, you found something to wear, and your feet held you when you stood. None of it feels like news. It's the floor the day is built on, and nobody thanks a floor. The Jewish morning service begins by thanking it anyway, one piece at a time: a short chain of blessings, each fitted to something a waking body just did. Today, the chain itself.
screen: `BEFORE COFFEE, A LOT WENT RIGHT.` → `NOBODY THANKS A FLOOR.` → `A CHAIN OF THANKS.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're called birchot hashachar, the blessings of the dawn. Each one opens with the same words, baruch atah, blessed are you, and then names one gift. Who opens the eyes of the blind. Who clothes the naked. Who raises up the bowed down. Who makes firm a person's steps. Where did they come from? The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty b, walks through a person's waking. When you hear the rooster, say this. When you open your eyes, say this. When you sit up, when you dress, when you stand, when your feet touch the ground, when you put on your shoes. A blessing for each motion, said at the moment it happened. So in the Talmud's telling, these blessings belong to the bedroom, not the synagogue. Over the centuries many communities moved them into the service and said them as a list. One explanation: hands weren't yet washed at the bedside, and not everyone knew the words, so the leader said them aloud and everyone answered amen. Maimonides didn't like the change. He held that each blessing belongs to its own moment. Today some people say a few at home as they wake, and many also say them together in the service. Either way, the order still follows a body getting up: hearing, seeing, sitting, dressing, standing, walking. Underneath is a simple rule. The Talmud teaches that a person shouldn't enjoy anything in this world without a blessing, and waking up is the first thing you enjoy. Sight and steady legs aren't treated as small just because they're common. The list is a way of noticing the basics before the day buries them.
screen: `BIRCHOT HASHACHAR: BLESSINGS OF DAWN.` · `A BLESSING FOR EACH MOTION.` · `FROM THE BEDROOM TO THE SERVICE.` · `NO JOY WITHOUT A BLESSING.` · then, large: `THANKS FOR THE BASICS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for three things your body does. Settle, and breathe. Start with the breath itself, going in and out without being asked. Then pick two more. Your eyes, taking in the room. Your hands, which have already done a hundred small jobs today. Your heartbeat. Your hearing. For each one, stay a few breaths and simply notice it working. If you pray, you can begin each with the words baruch atah, blessed are you. If you don't, a plain thank you is enough. The bell holds the time.
Birchot hashachar. The blessings of the dawn: a chain of short thanks for waking, seeing, dressing and standing.
Your line: thanks for the basics. Today, when you do one ordinary thing, open a door, tie a shoe, stand up from a chair, give it one second of thanks. Day five hundred forty-two.

543.title: The rooster's understanding
543.hook: the first morning blessing thanks God for giving the rooster sense to tell day from night
543.howItsDone: The blessing over the rooster is the first of the morning blessings in most Jewish prayer books; the Talmud ties it to hearing the rooster at dawn, and today it is said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birchot hashachar, the chain of blessings for a waking body. Your line was thanks for the basics. Which ordinary thing got its second of thanks? Today, the first link in the chain. Day five hundred forty-three.

Picture a town two thousand years ago. No alarm clock, no street lights, no glowing phone on the nightstand. Just dark, and then less dark, and somewhere before the sun is up, a rooster. Every house hears it. The baker hears it and gets up for the dough. The shepherd hears it and reaches for his cloak. That cry was the town's clock. So when the rabbis lined up the blessings for waking, the very first one wasn't about you at all. It was about the bird outside the window.
screen: `NO ALARM CLOCK.` → `THE ROOSTER WAS THE TOWN'S CLOCK.` → `THE FIRST BLESSING IS ABOUT A BIRD.`

segments.voice: The blessing says: blessed are you, who gave the sechvi understanding to tell day from night. The Talmud, in Berakhot, page sixty b, says to say it when you hear the rooster call. And the word sechvi is a puzzle. It shows up in the Bible only once, in the Book of Job, where God asks Job who gave understanding to the sechvi. Translators have never agreed what it means there. Some read it as the mind or the heart; the 1917 Jewish translation chose mind. But the Talmud, in tractate Rosh Hashanah, reports that in one region people called a rooster a sechvi. So the rabbis heard Job's question as: who taught the rooster to know when morning comes? Later commentators kept both meanings at once. The rooster knows night from day, and so does the human heart, if it's paying attention. The blessing thanks God for the bird, and for the mind that hears it. Notice what kind of understanding this is. Not cleverness. Not knowing facts. Binah, discernment: being able to tell one thing from another. It echoes the first day of creation, when God divides the light from the darkness. The day begins, in this prayer book, with a distinction. It's morning now. Night is over. Whatever happened in the dark doesn't have to set the tone for the light. That's a small thing to know, and a large one.
screen: `WHO GAVE THE SECHVI UNDERSTANDING?` · `A WORD FROM THE BOOK OF JOB.` · `THE ROOSTER, AND THE HEART.` · `BINAH: TELLING ONE THING FROM ANOTHER.` · then, large: `TELL DAY FROM NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for one sound that tells you the time. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes if you like, and let your ears go out to the edges of the room, then past them. Traffic, a bird, a neighbor's door, the hum of a fridge, wind. Wait until you find one sound that tells you something about this hour: morning, midday, evening, night. Stay with that one sound. Let it be your rooster. Notice that you knew what it meant without thinking. The bell holds the time.
The rooster's understanding. The first morning blessing: thanks for the creature, and the mind, that can tell day from night.
Your line: tell day from night. Today, when something from a bad night or a hard yesterday tries to follow you in, name it, and say to yourself: it's morning now. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: Opening blind eyes
544.hook: blessings for sight, freedom, clothing and steady steps
544.howItsDone: These blessings are part of the morning blessings said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service, and in many synagogues the leader chants them aloud while the congregation answers amen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rooster's understanding, and the first blessing of the morning. Your line was tell day from night. What did you leave behind in the dark? Today, the eyes open. Day five hundred forty-four.

Your eyes open in the morning and the room comes back. Ceiling, curtain, the chair with yesterday's clothes on it. It takes half a second, and you've done it every day of your life. Now listen to what the prayer book calls that half second. Not waking up. Not getting going. It calls it opening the eyes of the blind. And it keeps going in that key. Sitting up becomes setting the captive free. Getting dressed becomes clothing the naked. Big words, the words of rescue, for the smallest motions of a morning.
screen: `THE ROOM COMES BACK.` → `OPENING THE EYES OF THE BLIND.` → `BIG WORDS FOR SMALL MOTIONS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot, pairs each blessing with a motion. When you open your eyes: blessed are you, pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. When you sit up and stretch: matir asurim, who frees the bound, because a body stiff from sleep has just been let loose. When you dress: malbish arumim, who clothes the naked. When you stand up straight: zokef kefufim, who raises the bowed down. When you start to walk: who makes firm a person's steps. Where do these phrases come from? Several are lifted almost word for word from the Psalms. Psalm one hundred forty-six, in the old Jewish translation, says: "The LORD looseth the prisoners; the LORD openeth the eyes of the blind; the LORD raiseth up them that are bowed down." In the psalm, those are rescues: God lifting the people who have the least. The prayer book borrows that language for your own ordinary morning. Why? The Talmud elsewhere calls sleep a sixtieth part of death. Seen that way, every waking is a small return: from not seeing to seeing, from lying still to moving. And many people hear a second layer too. To say who opens the eyes of the blind is to remember that for some people, sight is not a given, and freedom isn't, and clothing isn't. The blessing thanks God for your morning in words that keep other people's mornings in view.
screen: `POKEACH IVRIM: WHO OPENS BLIND EYES.` · `A BLESSING FOR EACH MOTION.` · `BORROWED FROM PSALM 146.` · `YOUR MORNING, AND OTHERS' MORNINGS.` · then, large: `EYES OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing you can see. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes for a few breaths and sit in the dark. Then open them slowly, as if for the first time today. Let your gaze land on one thing. A cup, a plant, a patch of light on the wall, your own hand. Look at it longer than you normally would: its color, its edges, the shadow it throws. If you pray, you can say pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. If not, just keep looking. The bell holds the time.
Opening blind eyes. Pokeach ivrim: the morning blessing for sight, borrowed from a psalm about rescue.
Your line: eyes opened. Today, once, stop and really look at something you pass every day, and see one detail you've never noticed. Day five hundred forty-four.

545.title: Strength to the weary
545.hook: a later blessing thanks God for giving strength to the tired
545.tomorrow: The soul you gave me is pure
545.howItsDone: Most Jewish prayer books include the blessing 'who gives strength to the weary' among the morning blessings, often as the last of the series, said at home or at the start of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessings for sight, freedom and clothing, borrowed from a psalm. Your line was eyes opened. What did you see that you'd never noticed? Today, the blessing for people who wake up tired. Day five hundred forty-five.

Not everybody wakes up rested. The baby was up at three. The worry was up at four. Some mornings you open your eyes and the first thing you feel is how heavy your arms are. A prayer book that only thanked God for bright, bouncing mornings would leave a lot of people out. So it matters that near the end of the morning blessings, many prayer books carry one that seems written for exactly this person. It isn't in the Talmud's list at all. It came later, and it stuck.
screen: `NOT EVERYBODY WAKES UP RESTED.` → `THE BABY AT THREE.` → `A BLESSING THAT CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: The words are: blessed are you, hanoten laya'ef koach, who gives strength to the weary. The phrase is taken from the prophet Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation, chapter forty: "He giveth power to the faint." A few verses on, Isaiah promises that those who wait for God will renew their strength, and run, and not be weary. The word ya'ef means worn out from effort, the tiredness of someone who has been working or walking a long way. Here's the history. The Talmud's list of waking blessings doesn't include this one. It shows up in the medieval prayer books of France and Germany, and from there it spread. Some authorities hesitated. Rabbi Joseph Karo, the great codifier of the sixteenth century, was uneasy about a blessing the Talmud never mentions. But the people kept it, and today it sits in most prayer books, in many communities as the last of the morning blessings. Think about where it lands. After all the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes, one more line admits something honest: you're up, but you may not be full of energy. The blessing doesn't pretend otherwise. It doesn't say who makes the weary cheerful. It says who gives them strength, enough to begin. Sleep is treated as a gift that restores, and the morning starts by thanking God for what was restored, even if it's only partly.
screen: `HANOTEN LAYA'EF KOACH.` · `FROM ISAIAH 40.` · `NOT IN THE TALMUD'S LIST.` · `ENOUGH STRENGTH TO BEGIN.` · then, large: `STRENGTH TO THE WEARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest one minute, then begin. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Let your hands go heavy in your lap. Don't try to feel energetic; just admit how tired you actually are, right now, on a scale of one to ten. Then breathe slowly, and feel what's still there under the tiredness: a heartbeat, a breath, enough strength to sit here. If you pray, you can say hanoten laya'ef koach. When the bell comes, start the next thing you have to do, even slowly. The bell holds the time.
Strength to the weary. Hanoten laya'ef koach: a later morning blessing, from Isaiah, for everyone who wakes up tired.
Your line: strength to the weary. Today, notice one tired person near you, and take one small thing off their load: a dish, an errand, a minute of quiet. Day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: The soul you gave me is pure
546.hook: Elohai Neshamah: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure
546.howItsDone: Elohai neshamah is said each morning among the morning blessings, at home or in the synagogue; many people also say the short Modeh Ani on first waking and Elohai neshamah after washing their hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a later blessing for people who wake up tired. Your line was strength to the weary. Whose load did you lighten? Today, the end of this week, and the blessing for the soul. Day five hundred forty-six.

What's the first thing your mind says to you in the morning? For a lot of people it's a list of failures. You didn't finish that. You said the wrong thing. You're behind. The inner critic is often awake before you are. Now put next to that the line the Talmud says a person should say on waking, before the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes. It doesn't begin with what you did wrong. It doesn't begin with what you owe. It begins with one word about who you are: pure.
screen: `THE INNER CRITIC WAKES FIRST.` → `A DIFFERENT FIRST WORD.` → `PURE.`

segments.voice: The prayer is called Elohai neshamah, my God, the soul. In the Talmud, in Berakhot, it runs roughly like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me. You guard it within me, and one day you will take it from me, and return it in the time to come. As long as the soul is in me, I give thanks. And it ends: blessed are you, who restores souls to bodies. Now the word. Neshamah means soul, and it's close kin to the Hebrew word for breath. In Genesis, the old Jewish translation says God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Breath of life there is nishmat chayim. So when the prayer says you breathed it into me, it's pointing back to the first human, and to every breath since. Notice the order of the prayer. Before thanks, before requests, before any confession, it makes a statement: the soul is pure. Jewish teachers often point to this line to say that every person starts each morning with a soul that is clean. Mistakes are real, and the tradition takes repair very seriously. But the soul itself isn't the mistake. And the prayer is honest about death too: it says plainly that the soul will one day be taken. That's why waking is treated as a return. You got it back again this morning.
screen: `ELOHAI NESHAMAH: MY GOD, THE SOUL.` · `NESHAMAH: SOUL, AND BREATH.` · `PURE, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.` · `WAKING IS A RETURN.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS PURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe and say pure. Settle, and breathe. Feel the air come in through your nose, cool, and go out, warm. Each time you breathe in, think of the word neshamah, breath and soul together. Each time you breathe out, say the word pure, out loud or inside. If the critic starts its list, let it talk, and keep breathing under it. In, neshamah. Out, pure. Nothing to fix for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
